visible.summary:
Bali is Indonesia's most tolerant mainstream environment: 2026 travel guidance still describes a "live and let live" ethos, with gay-friendly life concentrated in Seminyak, Canggu and Ubud, and no criminal enforcement against foreign tourists recorded. That informality, however, is not protection. The national penal code brought into force in 2026 criminalises extramarital sex, including same-sex relations; LGBTQ+ travel advisories rate the island "Exercise Significant Caution", public displays of affection are discouraged for all couples, and same-sex marriage remains unrecognised.

A 2025 ethnographic study of the island's trans women (transpuan) communities pointedly challenges the "refuge" framing, documenting persistent misrecognition and systemic discrimination beneath the tolerant surface. Visitors should read Bali as relatively safer by local custom — with the new penal code, conservative local administration and documented structural discrimination setting the limits of that safety.
visible.tangentialFactors: Same-sex conduct provisions (KUHP Art. 412 cohabitation/sex outside marriage) reach trans visitors in couples or shared accommodation, complaint-based but newly available as a leverage tool in any police contact.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Bali's general tourism-hazard profile (traffic, surf, scams) is unrelated to trans risk; the island's relative safety is a social-fact, not a legal exemption.

sources.claim: Peer-reviewed article (Anthropology of the Middle East, 2025) on the 'precarious lives' of the transpuan (trans feminine) community in Indonesia based on four ethnographic case studies in Bali: documents how transpuan people navigate circumstances marked by both resistance and misrecognition and discrimination, challenging the narrative of victimhood while showing real precarity. For this record: academic ground-truth that Bali hosts a visible trans community living with precarity, discrimination, and informal resistance.

Travel guide (Gayborhood/Traven) on Bali: ranks the destination '6.3/10' with a legal score of 2.0, warning same-sex relations are criminalised in Indonesia and that LGBTQ+ travellers face legal risks; advises visitors to 'keep your love a little quieter' despite the island's tolerant reputation. For this record: practical traveller-facing warning that Bali's legal backdrop (Indonesian national law) carries criminalisation risk even where the local scene is accepting.

Travel guide (Mar 2026): Bali is broadly welcoming to LGBTQ+ travellers on a 'live and let live' basis, and same-sex relationships are not a criminal offence in Bali under Indonesian national law, though the new Criminal Code (KUHP, in effect Jan 2026) adds complexity; same-sex marriage is not legally recognised anywhere in Indonesia; Seminyak (Eat Street/Batu Belig), Canggu and Ubud are named as the most consistently LGBTQ+-friendly areas with active venues, while public displays of affection warrant discretion. For this record: current, specific traveller guidance for trans/LGBTQ visitors to Bali including the 2026 KUHP law change.

visible.summary:
No trans-specific legal measure or incident series is documented for this province in the surviving sources. The security environment, however, is not neutral: rights monitors recorded 138 acts of torture or ill-treatment in detention by police and military in the highland conflict zones of the island's western half between September 2021 and early 2025, "with almost no consequences", and a further surge of military deployments, fatal shootings and arbitrary detentions from August 2025, alongside internal displacement.

For any visitor — including a transgender one — contact with security forces in the highland districts carries a documented risk of arbitrary detention and mistreatment, and the surveillance environment raises the chance of being noticed and questioned. This is a general-population security finding, not evidence of trans-specific targeting.
visible.tangentialFactors: The new national KUHP (Jan 2026) applies fully in Papua; the region-specific factor is not an anti-LGBT bylaw (none found) but a documented security-force abuse pattern that worsens any police contact, including for gender-nonconforming travellers.

sources.claim: TAPOL briefing (July 2025): police and military in West Papua committed 138 recorded acts of torture or ill-treatment in detention in Maybrat and the Central Highlands (Sept 2021-Q1 2025) with almost no consequences; victims mostly males under 24 plus 7 women and 7 minors; arrests largely for alleged armed-group links or demonstrations; deaths during torture documented in operation areas; incidents catalogued on the 'Papuans Behind Bars' database.

Human Rights Monitor Papua Quarterly Report Q3 2025 (31 Oct 2025) on West Papua: documents killings, arbitrary detentions, torture and the failure of accountability mechanisms by security forces expanding across the territory, plus a healthcare crisis under scrutiny and arrests of protesters. Contains no trans/LGBTI-specific findings. For this record: indicates a high-violence, low-accountability security climate in West Papua relevant to overall traveller safety, but provides no trans-specific substance.

Since June 2021 Indonesia's Ministry of Home Affairs has run outreach issuing transgender Indonesians identification papers (KTP), and the page names Papua among the provinces whose trans residents have benefited (with Banten, West Java, Central Java, East Java, North Sumatra, South Sumatra, South Sulawesi and Lampung); only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors are recognised, with birth-gender printed unless a court order was already obtained. The same page's national-framework facts apply in Papua: the 2022 penal-code amendment criminalising sexual activity outside marriage (up to one year in prison) takes effect on 2 January 2026, same-sex marriage is not recognised, and customary laws may apply. For this record: evidence that trans people in Papua may obtain identity documents through the national outreach programme, and the national legal framework a trans visitor stands under while in the province.

visible.summary:
On 19 July 2026 Palembang's city government announced it was preparing a regulation rejecting LGBT, presented as local follow-through on Presidential Regulation (Perpres) No. 111 of 2025 on the national defence policy 2025-2029, which lists the 'spread of LGBTQ culture' among non-military threats; Mayor Ratu Dewa made the announcement in the courtyard of the Grand Mosque. The regulation remains in preparation, not enacted, with no specified penalty; no enforcement event is documented for this province. South Sumatra is one of the eight provinces analysed in OutRight's discriminatory-regulation mapping, and its neighbour Lampung saw a documented Satpol PP raid on three transwomen (November 2018) - the Sumatran belt is where local enforcement is consolidating.

The deviation from the national score is small and below it, similar to South Sulawesi (0.13). The Perpres 111/2025 framing elevates local anti-LGBT measures from moral panic to national-defence doctrine - the August 2026 ABC reporting links the 'rule that deems them a threat' to a wave of street attacks on trans women, though it cautions the trend cannot yet be confirmed - but without an enacted local penalty the traveler-facing risk here remains prospective. It sits above West Sumatra (0.11), which has a live bylaw with specified sanctions.
visible.tangentialFactors: Perpres 111/2025's non-military-threat framing and the new national KUHP (Jan 2026) apply to all South Sumatra visitors regardless of the pending local regulation - the local fact is the announced rejection rule, the national facts carry the present legal exposure.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Palembang's general urban-crime and traffic profile is unrelated to trans risk; the documented violence wave (Bogor) is in a different province and is used here only as the national trend context.

sources.claim: RRI Palembang (20 Jul 2026): Palembang city government is preparing a regulation rejecting LGBT, presented as local follow-through on Presidential Regulation No. 111 of 2025 - the national defence policy 2025-2029 listing the 'spread of LGBTQ culture' among non-military threats. Mayor Ratu Dewa announced the move in the Grand Mosque courtyard on 19 July 2026; the regulation is in preparation, no penalty specified, no enforcement documented.

OutRight Action International, 'Creeping Criminalisation': the mapping of discriminatory regional regulations in eight Indonesian provinces includes South Sumatra, evidencing the province's place in the regional-bylaw belt that drafts like Palembang's extend.

ABC News (15 Aug 2026): an attack on a trans woman in Bogor on 15 July 2026 was one of 10 attacks on trans women there between 30 March and 15 July 2026, with 45 victim-survivors per advocacy group data - victims punched, kicked, some stripped. The piece ties the wave to Presidential Regulation No. 111 of 2025 (effective October 2025) classifying the 'spread of LGBTQ culture' as a non-military threat, while quoting an official insisting it is a broader defence policy not aimed at LGBTQI people.

visible.summary: No criminalisation of trans presence. The state congress created an administrative legal gender recognition procedure in a 2022 Civil Code reform; after the Supreme Court struck down its adults-only limit in June 2023, a new reform passed in 2024 extended recognition to children and adolescents. In May 2022 the congress also added a penal-code chapter "Crimes against Sexual Orientation, Gender Identity and Expression". The counterweight is Tijuana: the state attorney general publicly warned of a serial killer of women in prostitution there (at least 3 victims; suspect arrested July 2023 after an Interpol notice and FBI cooperation), only 22 of 278 killed women in the state were classed as feminicides, and a 2021 burning of a trans woman's body in her Tijuana home is recorded within that pattern. Mixed: protective law, under-counted lethal risk concentrated in one border city.
visible.tangentialFactors: The Tijuana serial-killer pattern centred on people in sex work - victims' gender-nonconforming presentation is part of the targeting, so it reads as bias-adjacent violence, not pure criminal opportunity.
visible.localsOnly: The 2022/2024 legal gender recognition reforms and the penal-code hate-crime chapter operate on resident documents and prosecutions.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch state-by-state tracker on legal gender recognition in Mexico (March 2025), covering which of the 32 states have legislated an administrative procedure and the Supreme Court rulings that drove expansion. For Baja California: 2022 Civil Code reform created an administrative legal gender recognition procedure for adults; the Supreme Court invalidated its 18-years requirement in June 2023; a 2024 reform followed.

Human Rights Watch report 'I Just Want to Contribute to Society' (6 March 2024) on Tabasco: no legal gender recognition procedure there exposes trans people to institutional mistreatment - the August 2023 killing of activist Karina Gomez remained unsolved, hate-motivation provisions are absent from Tabasco's criminal code, and healthcare staff routinely out patients by calling legal names. Baseline for how a non-reforming state behaves.

Guardian report (24 July 2024) on Mexico City making transfemicide a crime with sentences up to 70 years (the 'Paola Buenrostro law', approved 18 July 2024), in one of Latin America's deadliest settings for trans people; over 95% of homicides nationally went unpunished in 2022.

HRW's state-by-state survey records that Baja California's congress enacted a 2022 reform to the Civil Code creating an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition for adults; in June 2023 Mexico's Supreme Court struck down the law's adults-only requirement because it did not recognize the rights of transgender children and adolescents; and in 2024 the state congress passed a new reform establishing a procedure for individuals under 18 and expanding legal gender recognition to non-binary people. This is the authoritative confirmation of the exact legal-recognition timeline the record states for Baja California.

Zeta Tijuana (8 July 2023, Rosario Mosso Castro) reports that Brayan Rivera was presented on 6 July 2023 before US Judge Karen L. Stevenson in provisional detention for extradition, accused by Mexico of the feminicide of Ángela Carolina Acosta, killed on 24 January 2022 in room 404 of Hotel Cascadas beside Bar Hong Kong in Tijuana's tolerance zone; probable cause was determined on 29 June 2023 by the US federal court, and he was arrested at his parents' Downey, California home, where officers found the Hotel Cascadas rent receipt and rope and gloves. At a 7 July 2023 press conference the Baja California attorney general called the 30-year-old a serial perpetrator, said extradition could take from 15 days to two years, and that nearly a decade of open case files were being reviewed; the investigation had linked him to at least three feminicides - Ángela (January 2022), Elizabeth (14 February), and Karen, 28 (30 August 2021, Motel Hacienda Soler). This is the dated, local-press verification of the serial-killer counterweight in the record's Tijuana risk picture.

Zeta Tijuana (8 March 2025, Rosario Mosso Castro) reports that under Baja California Governor Marina del Pilar Ávila, 1,179 women have been killed in the state while only 110 cases were typified as feminicide - a small share that underscores under-classification of lethal violence against women - and that female economic participation in the state stood at roughly 46-47%, 14th of 32 states. This state-level data supports the record's 'under-counted lethal risk' characterization for Baja California, complementing the Tijuana-specific serial-killer case.

visible.summary:
No State of Mexico-specific figures, articles or compliance records are supported by the vetted sources for this map. The national picture governs: by March 2025 an international human-rights organization counted 22 of Mexico's 32 states as having legislated legal gender-recognition procedures, with six state legislatures enacting none; a March 2024 report documents that where no procedure exists, trans people face police stops, denied documents and institutional mistreatment.

Transfeminicide has become a criminal category in some states — the capital imposes up to 70 years — against more than 95% homicide impunity nationally, and reporting finds convictions lag the statutes. For a visitor, this state's own documented record is thin: expect the country-wide picture rather than verified local protections or verified local hostility.
visible.tangentialFactors: The lethality ranking comes from national hate-crime tallies that count all LGBT+ victims together - violence targeting gay men and lesbians forms part of the state's numbers.
visible.localsOnly: The unremedied adults-only gap in the recognition procedure is a resident documentation problem; visitors carry federally issued passports.

sources.claim: National framework (HRW, 31 Mar 2025): legal gender recognition in Mexico is set state-by-state — as of March 2025, 22 of the 32 states had legislated an administrative recognition procedure, two more run one in practice without enactment, six legislatures have enacted none, and only seven states extend recognition to children. Mexico's Supreme Court set binding guidelines for the states and extended the right to minors in 2022; the Inter-American Court likewise requires a simple, accessible procedure. HRW documents the consequences where no procedure exists (identity-document mismatch driving discrimination in schools, medical clinics and the labour market, incidents recorded in Guanajuato and Tabasco). For this record: the national mosaic, not any locally enacted certainty, is the operative framework.

HRW/Community Center for Inclusion report (6 Mar 2024) on a Mexican state lacking a legal gender-recognition procedure, documented in Tabasco: without identity documents matching a trans person's gender, every document request or appearance scrutiny carries violence, harassment and humiliation risk, excluding trans people from employment, health services, education and financial transactions; context includes the Aug 2023 murder of trans woman Karina Gomez in Villahermosa and more than 95% of homicides nationally going unpunished in 2022. For this record it is the operative evidence of what 'state law silent' means for trans people on the ground.
